article.headline: The Breadth-Thrust Regime That Powered a 26% Gain Has Lapsed
article.lede: On May 13, 2026, a twelve-month statistical tailwind for U.S. equities quietly expired. The signal — Grant Hawkridge's 20-Day High Breadth Thrust — fires when 55% or more of S&P 500 stocks simultaneously reach a new 20-day closing high, marking unusually broad buying pressure rather than a narrow mega-cap surge. The regime that launched in May 2025 delivered roughly 26%; whether the indicator reloads in coming weeks will decide whether that tailwind persists or quietly disappears.
article.body:
The indicator tracks a single condition: what share of the S&P 500's roughly 500 component stocks are simultaneously trading at a fresh 20-day closing high. When that share clears 55% — a rare occurrence requiring synchronized buying across sectors — Hawkridge designates the following twelve months a *breadth thrust regime*. Within that window, historical data shows the index has never been lower a year later. Willie Delwiche, a *CMT* and *CFA* who runs Hi Mount Research, has documented the same phenomenon independently: “all the net gains for the S&P 500 and then some since the late 1990s have come within the year following a breadth thrust.”

The most recent trigger arrived in mid-May 2025, during the sharp rebound from a tariff-shock low. President Trump’s April 2, 2025 tariff announcement sent the S&P 500 down roughly 19% in days; the subsequent reversal was broad enough to fire multiple breadth signals in rapid succession. The classical *Zweig Breadth Thrust* — which measures the ratio of NYSE advancing issues to total issues over a ten-day rolling window — triggered April 24, 2025, with the index near $5,485. Hawkridge’s 55% threshold fired roughly three weeks later, near $5,886, launching the regime. Over the following twelve months the index climbed past 7,500, a gain of roughly 26% — well above the historical average of approximately 20% following prior triggers.

Expiry does not guarantee a drawdown, but the precedent is cautionary. Both recent expirations in Hawkridge’s dataset were followed by corrections: the October 2022 regime expired October 2023 and a sell-off ensued; the November 2023 regime expired November 2024, feeding the deterioration that the April 2025 tariff shock then extended. As analyst Martin Schwoerer summarized the framework: “You’re good for around twelve months, and then you’re not.”

As of expiry, internal *market breadth* did not appear poised for a quick reload. Thrasher Analytics reported its Breadth Thrust Composite at zero in early May 2026, with more S&P 500 constituents trading below their 20-day moving averages than above. Should the 55% threshold be breached again in coming weeks, a new twelve-month regime would formally begin and the historical tailwind would resume. If not, the market enters what Hawkridge terms the “easy money phase over” — a regime-less state in which the statistical foundation for equity gains is considerably thinner.

concepts.definition: A signal that fires when an unusually large share of stocks in an index simultaneously surge to new short-term highs, or when advancing issues vastly outnumber decliners, indicating that buying is broad-based rather than concentrated in a few names. Breadth thrusts are treated as leading indicators of durable bull-market phases rather than narrow, fragile rallies.

Hawkridge’s term for the twelve-month window that begins after a 20-Day High Breadth Thrust fires. Historical data shows the S&P 500 has been higher at the end of every such window in his dataset. When the window closes without a new thrust, the statistical safety net formally lapses — not a sell signal, but the removal of a historically reliable tailwind.

A classical breadth signal created by Martin Zweig that fires when the ratio of NYSE advancing issues to total issues (advancing plus declining) climbs from below 0.40 to above 0.615 within ten trading days. It has triggered roughly 20 times since 1950 and has been followed by positive S&P 500 returns at both the six- and twelve-month marks in all cases.

A collective measure of how many individual securities are participating in a market move, as distinct from how much the index itself has moved. Strong breadth means gains are distributed across many stocks; narrow breadth — where a small number of large-caps do most of the work — is often treated as a warning sign for the durability of a trend.

An aggregated indicator tracked by Thrasher Analytics that combines multiple individual breadth thrust signals into a single score. A reading of zero means no active thrust signals are firing across the basket of indicators that make up the composite, suggesting conditions for a new regime trigger are absent.

A professional credential awarded by the CMT Association to analysts who demonstrate mastery of technical analysis — the study of price charts, momentum, volume, and market structure. It is the primary professional designation in the field of technical analysis, roughly analogous to the CFA for fundamental investment analysts.

A credential awarded by the CFA Institute after candidates pass three rigorous exams covering investment analysis, portfolio management, and ethics. One of the most widely respected qualifications in the investment management industry, requiring several years of professional experience alongside the exams.

poster_granthawkridge.blurb: Grant Hawkridge is a self-described market chartist and enthusiast who posts technical analysis threads on US equities indices ($SPY, $SPX, $NYA, $COMPX). His work focuses on inter-market cycle analysis — tracking the sequential roll-overs of bonds, stocks, and commodities — and he references voices like @allstarcharts as part of his analytical framework. His profile bio ('Golf, cigars, whisky & looking at charts') signals an engaged hobbyist/independent analyst rather than a credentialed professional. Follower count is not available from the sources provided.
